newsitem.title: USA: US, German jobs data has U.S. pundits eying rates.
newsitem.headline: US, German jobs data has U.S. pundits eying rates.

text.p: Recent jobs reports may leave the door open for a U.S. rate hike and an ease in Germany, economists said, but a strong dollar versus the mark may help keep monetary policy on hold in Germany.
Economists noted the 271,000 gain in U.S. non-farm payrolls in January and the fact that average hourly earnings were up 5.5 percent on a three-month basis and 3.8 percent on a year-over-year basis.
"The pressure is still on the (Federal Reserve) to respond," said Alan Ruskin, chief economist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
"The data are still consistent with an economy running at least at 3.0 percent, which is above most estimates of the speed limit at which point inflation pressures are likely to rise," Ruskin added.
Some investors were cheered on Friday by news that average hourly earnings had inched up one cent to $12.06 in January.
Yet Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures said, "The fact that it's still up 3.8 percent from a year ago, I think, is more meaningful and it's headed higher."
Tainer said there was more likelihood of a Fed tightening in March or at the following meeting in May.
The policy setting arm of the U.S. central bank will next meet on March 25 and then again on May 20.

Still, Tainer said, the longer the Fed waits, the less likely it will need to tighten credit partly because of the impact from weaker exports. Furthermore, a strong dollar will lessen inflationary pressures.

Last week, the Fed and the Bundesbank both left rates unchanged. The German government also reported last week that the ranks of the jobless swelled to a new post war record of 4.66 million in January. Some analysts, however, were careful to note that harsh weather exaggerated the data.
"There has been some debate (over) whether they would or they wouldn't, but I think there certainly is room for the Bundesbank to ease," Tainer said.
Ruskin noted that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has hinted at the need to tighten fiscal policy.

"And if they are going to have to tighten fiscal policy even more because of a weak economy, then they are going to implicity (have) the need to ease monetary policy as well, somewhat more than we previously expected," Ruskin said.
"There's certainly a bias in terms of interest rates going down still in Germany," he said.
